title: Problems Are the Main Show
subtitle: The anxiety is information, and the route back to meaning runs straight through the problem

sections.content: You can have ninety percent of what you want and still be miserable. Problems don't occupy their fair share of our attention — a handful of recurring, unresolved irritations will colonize an otherwise good life until they become the only thing you can see. The modern advice is to reframe: practice gratitude, trust the process, enjoy the ride. I'd argue the opposite. Sometimes the anxiety is information, and the only honest route back to meaning runs straight through the problem itself.

I should say who this is for. It's for people in their twenties and thirties who haven't yet closed off their options — and I'd include most people from a low socioeconomic background in a developed country in that, because the potential there is still considerable and the deciding factor is usually whether you engage with what's holding you back or decide not to look at it. It is not written for people whose circumstances have genuinely run out of slack. I don't have much to offer them, and I'd rather admit that than pretend the essay stretches further than it does.

The mechanism is attention. An unsolved problem doesn't sit quietly in a corner — it idles in the background, burning cycles, and the more of them you accumulate, the less capacity you have to address any single one. This is why the standard advice to focus on what matters most can backfire: sometimes solving ten small problems is what buys you the bandwidth to face the large one. And when a problem clears, something takes its place. Not necessarily something good — but the odds improve. You've re-rolled the dice, which is more than you can say for living alongside it.

But you can't run this as a cost-benefit analysis, because the person drowning in problems is precisely the person who can't estimate the costs or the payoffs. So don't try. Attempt the problem anyway, because the attempt is the education. Your problems are a diagnostic — they show you exactly where you're thin, where you need reinforcing. Solving one doesn't just remove an irritant; it converts you into someone with a wider range.

So why don't people solve solvable problems? Because we're built to hold steady. When things are tolerable, something in us conserves energy and stays put — which was excellent advice when calories were scarce and novelty was dangerous. It's poor advice now. The modern world offers more variety than any individual can sample, and rewards the ability to handle complexity. I notice this in myself with something as trivial as software: I resist trying anything new, and then almost every time I'm nudged into it, the new thing turns out to be better than what I'd been stubbornly using. My defaults are reliably worse than what's available. There's no reason to think that stops at software.

There's a second miscalibration, too. Most of what we now encounter wasn't put there by an indifferent nature — it was put there by someone who wanted us to use it and enjoy it. In the wild, an unfamiliar mushroom might kill you. In a supermarket, that same mushroom was grown by someone who worked hard at it, and it's on the shelf because somebody's analysis suggested people like you would enjoy it. The same goes for the buttons you never click in software you use every day. Someone spent months building those. The fact that you can get by without them says nothing about what they'd give you. In a designed world, curiosity is nearly free — and our inherited caution is charging us for it anyway.

Here's what actually holds people still. It isn't cost in any measurable sense — it's exposure. Clicking the unknown button risks almost nothing, and people still don't click it. Ask why, and you find something subtler than caution: the vague dread of discovering you've been doing it wrong all along. And if it goes sideways, you might have to call a colleague over and admit you don't understand your own tools. The price of a problem doesn't scale with how hard it is to solve. It scales with how much solving it forces you to look at your own inadequacy. Which is why the private version — practising badly where nobody can see — feels affordable, and the public version costs so much more. The price of getting better is being visibly worse first. Freedom asks for discipline, thinness asks for hunger, competence asks that you look incompetent for a while. There's no version where you get the upside without tolerating its opposite.

There's a version of this that used to be survivable. You built real skill early, then the job changed shape — a cabinetmaker becomes someone who negotiates with suppliers and manages a roster, and one day it's been a year since he touched a chisel. That's not laziness; it's the business making other demands. But the ground keeps moving. New steels hold an edge longer, the industry standard shifts to a machine he's never run, and he's the one deciding which one to buy. Staying current doesn't mean keeping every skill sharp — nobody has the hours. It means keeping contact with reality, either by putting your own hands on the tool for a while, or by building enough trust with the people who do that they'll tell you the truth. The catch is that those people are usually junior to you. Someone with twenty years in can routinely learn something from someone with two, and refusing that conversation on the grounds of status robs you of exactly the information you need. Lose contact with the ground and you don't just fall behind on technique — you lose the ability to tell which of your problems are solvable. You can tell when this is happening, because unexpected things start happening. Surprise is the reading on the instrument: it means your model of the world has come apart from the world, and every action you take is producing a result you didn't order. That's information you want revealed early and cheaply rather than late and expensively — which is one more argument for engaging with small problems while they're still small.

So which problems are actually yours? There's a test better than authenticity and better than approval: does this dissolve problems, now or later? It cuts both ways — sometimes it justifies conforming, sometimes defying. I behave one way as a father to a young child, another with my wife, another alone, and none of that is inconsistency. I've chosen a variant of myself in service of the marriage, largely in service of problems we've anticipated and don't intend to have. And for sorting the real problems from the noise, extrapolate. Take the last bad ten minutes and imagine it recurring daily for twenty years. Could you live a satisfactory life? If yes, it's an irritation. If no, it needs your attention now. The same instrument tells you when to let something go: you might dislike something about your car, but if you're only driving it another year, your concern is better spent elsewhere.

There's no proof any of this pays off. I believe it has to, which isn't the same thing — and it's worth admitting that the floor of this position is faith rather than argument. What I can say is that the alternative is a guaranteed loop: if you don't transform, your experience becomes repetitious, and you die having sampled less of what was available than you might have. And you're never doing this alone. Whether there's anything worth engaging with when you get there is partly a function of your effort, and partly the inheritance of other people's successes. Some of us are simply unlucky. If your attempts were genuine — informed, honest, occasionally wrong in ways you couldn't have foreseen — then self-respect is the appropriate response, and you're not disqualified from enjoying what the world offers. The world doesn't require everyone to succeed. It requires that those who do tell the rest of us what they found.
